DBQ-A.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Protestant Reformation changed the relationship between rulers and the church in the Holy Roman Empire between 1517 and 1555.
DBQ-A.scoringNotes: Accept as context: the weak emperor and many territorial princes, medieval papal and episcopal jurisdiction and wealth, earlier conflicts over church revenue, the printing press. Accept as outside evidence: Diet of Worms 1521, Peasants' War 1524-25, Schmalkaldic League, protection of Luther by the Saxon elector, Charles V's wars. For sourcing, credit an explanation of why an author's position, audience or purpose (for example a council justifying a seizure of property, a bishop who lost revenue, peasants appealing to Scripture) bears on how the document should be used. Documents 1-6 only.

sources.title: Document 1 - Letter from a Saxon court official to his prince, 1521 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The Emperor's edict demands that the monk Luther be seized, yet his pamphlets are read aloud in every market town in your lands. If you hand him over without a hearing, I fear the townspeople will rise. I advise Your Grace to keep him safe and let the learned decide whether his teaching agrees with Scripture.

sources.title: Document 2 - Minutes of the council of an imperial free city, 1525 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The council has resolved that the preachers of this city shall teach only what Scripture contains. The convents are closed and their property is placed under the council's treasury, from which the pastors and the poor will be paid. This keeps the common people calm, and no bishop outside these walls shall command our clergy.

sources.title: Document 3 - Demands drawn up by peasant villagers of Upper Swabia, 1525 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Each parish should choose its own pastor, who shall preach the gospel plainly. Serfdom should end, for Christ shed his blood for all alike. If any of these demands is shown by the Word of God to be wrong, we will withdraw it.

sources.title: Document 4 - Letter from a Lutheran prince to the bishop of his territory, 1528 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Since no church order exists in my lands, I have appointed visitors, councillors and learned men to inspect every parish, its pastor and its school. As the bishops have not done this, I act in this emergency as the guardian of my subjects' souls. Your jurisdiction over my territory is suspended until a general council meets.

sources.title: Document 5 - Complaint of a Catholic bishop to the Emperor, 1530 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The princes have taken the revenues of our churches, forbidden the Mass, and now claim to judge doctrine themselves. They say they obey Your Majesty, yet they take from the Church what has belonged to it for a thousand years. If this goes on, no one will be bound to obey either bishop or Emperor.

sources.title: Document 6 - Summary of the Peace of Augsburg, 1555 (ALTON-composed summary)
sources.body: The Peace allows each imperial prince or city to choose between Catholic and Lutheran worship for its territory. Subjects who do not accept the choice may sell their property and move elsewhere. Other Protestant groups, such as the Calvinists and Anabaptists, are not covered.

DBQ-B.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which industrialization changed the lives of working people in Britain between 1780 and 1850.
DBQ-B.scoringNotes: Accept as context: rural and domestic production, enclosure, growth of the cotton trade, early machines. Accept as outside evidence: Luddites, Factory Act of 1833, Ten Hours Act of 1847, Poor Law of 1834, Chartism, Peterloo, railways, Corn Laws. For sourcing, credit an explanation of why an author's position or purpose (for example a mill owner opposing shorter hours, weavers petitioning for protection, an artisan recruiting for a political movement) bears on how the document should be used. Documents 1-6 only.

sources.title: Document 1 - Testimony of a cotton-mill owner to a parliamentary committee, 1832 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: My mill runs twelve hours a day with an hour and a half for meals. Children from ten years old earn about four shillings a week and are healthy and well fed. If Parliament forced shorter hours, I could not compete with foreign mills, and the families would lose the wages they depend upon.

sources.title: Document 2 - Petition of handloom weavers to Parliament, 1811 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Twenty years ago a weaver could keep his family comfortably on his loom. Since the mills with power looms began to undersell us, our wages have fallen by half, and many of us cannot buy bread. We ask that Parliament fix a minimum price for our work.

sources.title: Document 3 - Population of a northern manufacturing town (ALTON-composed approximate figures)
Document 4 - Report of a physician on a manufacturing district, 1842 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: In the crowded courts where the labourers live, the streets are unpaved and without drains, and many families share one privy. The average age at death among labourers here is seventeen, while among the professional classes it is thirty-eight. Fever returns every year.

sources.title: Document 5 - Letter from a London artisan to a workers' newspaper, 1838 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The Reform Act gave the vote to shopkeepers and mill owners but not to us, who make the nation's wealth. Without a vote we cannot shape the laws on factory hours or the new poor-houses. We therefore support the People's Charter, which would give every man a vote.

sources.title: Document 6 - Report of a factory inspector, 1840s (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The law now limits children under thirteen to eight hours a day, but there are too few inspectors to visit every mill. Parents often swear that their children are older than they are, because the family cannot do without the wage. In the mills I visited, the hours of women and children are now shorter than a decade ago.

LEQ-A.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Scientific Revolution changed European views of authority between 1550 and 1700.
LEQ-A.scoringNotes: Accept as context: reliance on Aristotle, Ptolemy and Galen in universities, the Church's use of them in theology, Renaissance humanism and the printing press. Accept as evidence: Copernicus 1543, Vesalius, Kepler, Galileo and his 1633 condemnation, Bacon, Descartes, Harvey, Newton's Principia 1687, the Royal Society 1660, the persistent religious faith of many scientists. Facts must be accurate to be credited.

LEQ-B.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Congress of Vienna and its settlement maintained stability in Europe between 1815 and 1850.
LEQ-B.scoringNotes: Accept as context: the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars and the victors' fear of renewed revolution and French dominance. Accept as evidence: Metternich and Castlereagh, restoration of the Bourbons, balance of power and strengthened buffer states, German Confederation, Concert of Europe, Carlsbad Decrees 1819, interventions in Naples and Piedmont 1820-21, Greek independence, July Revolution and Belgian independence 1830, revolutions of 1848, no general war among great powers until 1853. Facts must be accurate to be credited.

SAQ-A.prompt: Answer parts A, B and C, labeling each (A), (B) and (C). (A) Identify ONE argument the author makes about how trade in the Indies should be conducted. (B) Explain ONE way the organization of European trading companies in the 1600s supported the approach described in the passage. (C) Explain ONE effect of European chartered-company trade on societies in Asia between 1600 and 1750.
SAQ-A.scoringNotes: A: the author argues that force (fortified posts and ships) may be used when treaties fail, that exclusive purchase of spices is the goal, or that private trade must be banned. B: joint-stock financing pooled many investors' money, and a state charter granted a monopoly and the right to arm ships and build forts. C: acceptable effects include displacement or coercion of local traders and rulers (for example the Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands in 1621, Portuguese and Dutch control of ports such as Malacca), monopoly arrangements imposed on producers, and fortified trading posts. Vague statements that companies 'changed Asia' earn no point.

sources.title: Passage - Instruction of the directors of a trading company to its governor in the Indies, 1620 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Trade in the Indies is not to be pursued by gentle means alone. Where the local rulers will not grant us the exclusive purchase of cloves and nutmeg, you shall secure it by treaty if you can and by fortified posts and ships if you must. Let no private man trade on his own account.
